\begin{annexitem}{annex:p01-bpi-duality}{thm:p01-bpi-duality}{Choice-free filter and ideal calculus}
\begin{proof}
For \(E\subseteq B\), put
\[
 F_E=\{b\in B:\text{for some }n\in\mathbb N\text{ and }a_1,\ldots,a_n\in E,
                    \ \bigwedge_{k=1}^{n}a_k\leq_B b\}.
\]
The empty meet gives \(1_B\in F_E\); a one-member meet gives
\(E\subseteq F_E\). Upward closure follows from transitivity of
\(\leq_B\). If two finite meets witness \(b,c\in F_E\), their
combined finite list witnesses \(b\wedge c\in F_E\). Hence \(F_E\)
is a filter. Every filter containing \(E\) contains each such finite
meet and everything above it, so contains \(F_E\). Finally,
\(0_B\in F_E\) iff one witnessing meet is zero, proving the
properness criterion, including the empty-list case.

For clarity, the Boolean identities used next follow from the declared
axioms, without a representation theorem. If \(r\wedge s=0_B\), then
\(r=r\wedge(s\vee\neg s)=r\wedge\neg s\), so
\(r\leq_B\neg s\); the converse follows by meeting with \(s\).
Thus \(a\leq_B b\) implies \(\neg b\leq_B\neg a\).
Complements are unique: if \(x,y\) both complement \(a\), then
\(x=x\wedge(a\vee y)=x\wedge y\), and symmetrically
\(y=x\wedge y\). Distribution verifies that \(\neg a\wedge\neg b\)
has zero meet and total join one with \(a\vee b\); it is therefore
\(\neg(a\vee b)\). Double complementation follows from uniqueness,
and gives the dual De Morgan identity. Consequently complement reverses
Boolean order and interchanges meets and joins. Thus
\(d(F)\) contains \(0_B\); if \(\neg a\in d(F)\) and
\(b\leq_B\neg a\), then \(a\leq_B\neg b\), so
\(\neg b\in F\) and \(b\in d(F)\). Also
\(\neg a\vee\neg c=\neg(a\wedge c)\in d(F)\) for
\(a,c\in F\). Therefore \(d(F)\) is an ideal. The same argument
with the operations interchanged takes ideals to filters.
Since \(d(d(E))=E\) and \(d\) preserves inclusion, this is the
stated bijection. Moreover \(1_B\in d(F)\) iff \(0_B\in F\).
Applying this bijection to the generated-filter argument proves that the
ideal generated by \(E\) is exactly
\(\{b:b\leq_B\bigvee_{k=1}^{n}a_k\text{ for a finite list in }E\}\),
with empty join \(0_B\).

Let \(U\) be a maximal proper filter. It cannot contain both
\(a\) and \(\neg a\), since their meet is zero. If \(a\notin U\),
the filter generated by \(U\cup\{a\}\) is improper by maximality.
Combining the finitely many members from \(U\) in a witnessing list
gives \(u\in U\) with \(u\wedge a=0_B\). (A witness not using
\(a\) would contradict properness.) The identity
\(u=(u\wedge a)\vee(u\wedge\neg a)\) implies
\(u\leq_B\neg a\), and hence \(\neg a\in U\).
Thus \(U\) decides complements. Conversely, if a proper filter decides
complements, a larger proper filter containing some \(a\notin U\)
would also contain \(\neg a\in U\), an impossibility. It is maximal.

Decision implies filter primeness: if \(a,b\notin U\), then
\(\neg a,\neg b\in U\), so
\(\neg(a\vee b)\in U\) and \(a\vee b\notin U\).
Conversely, filter primeness applied to
\(a\vee\neg a=1_B\in U\), together with properness, gives
exactly-one decision. For any filter,
\(a\wedge b\in U\) iff both \(a,b\in U\), by closure and
upward closure. Consequently decision and primeness give all the equations
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \chi_U(0_B)&=0,&\chi_U(1_B)&=1,\\
 \chi_U(\neg a)&=\neg\chi_U(a),&
 \chi_U(a\wedge b)&=\chi_U(a)\wedge\chi_U(b),\\
 \chi_U(a\vee b)&=\chi_U(a)\vee\chi_U(b).&&
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the operations on the right are in \(\mathbf2\). Conversely a
characteristic homomorphism has zero excluded, one included, meet closure
and upward closure (apply it to \(a\wedge b=a\)); its complement
equation gives decision, so it characterizes an ultrafilter.

For an ultrafilter \(U\), an element \(b\) lies in \(d(U)\) iff
\(\neg b\in U\), iff \(b\notin U\). Thus \(P=d(U)=B\setminus U\)
is a proper ideal. If \(a\wedge b\in P\), then
\(\neg a\vee\neg b\in U\), so one of \(\neg a,\neg b\) lies
in \(U\); hence one of \(a,b\) lies in \(P\).
Conversely a prime ideal \(P\) contains at least one of \(a,\neg a\),
because it contains their zero meet, and not both, because it excludes
their join \(1_B\). Its dual filter therefore decides complements and
is an ultrafilter; again it is \(B\setminus P\). Inclusion-preserving
duality takes maximal proper filters to maximal proper ideals. This also
proves that prime ideals are maximal, and that a maximal proper ideal is
prime by taking its dual filter. All families used are subsets of sets and
all witness combinations are finite; no choice function has been used.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p01-bpi-quotient}{thm:p01-bpi-quotient}{Boolean quotient without representative choices}
\begin{proof}
First note the elementary identity
\[
 e\wedge(a\mathbin{\triangle}b)=0_B
 \quad\text{iff}\quad e\wedge a=e\wedge b.
\]
For the forward implication, distribute \(e\wedge a\) across
\(b\vee\neg b\) and \(e\wedge b\) across \(a\vee\neg a\).
The two difference terms vanish, leaving both sides equal to
\(e\wedge a\wedge b\). For the reverse implication substitute the
equal terms in each difference summand; it then contains the meet of an
element with its complement and is zero. In particular
\(\neg(a\mathbin{\triangle}b)\wedge a
=\neg(a\mathbin{\triangle}b)\wedge b\).

Reflexivity and symmetry of \(\sim_I\) follow from
\(a\mathbin{\triangle}a=0_B\) and symmetry of the displayed
expression. For transitivity, suppose
\(a\mathbin{\triangle}b,b\mathbin{\triangle}c\in I\) and set
\(e=\neg(a\mathbin{\triangle}b)\wedge
       \neg(b\mathbin{\triangle}c)\).
Then \(e\wedge a=e\wedge b=e\wedge c\). The identity implies
\(e\wedge(a\mathbin{\triangle}c)=0_B\), so
\[
 a\mathbin{\triangle}c\leq_B\neg e
  =(a\mathbin{\triangle}b)\vee(b\mathbin{\triangle}c)\in I.
\]
Downward closure gives transitivity.

If \(a\sim_I b\) and \(c\sim_I d\), use
\(e=\neg(a\mathbin{\triangle}b)\wedge
       \neg(c\mathbin{\triangle}d)\).
On meeting with \(e\), both inputs agree. Distribution shows that their
joins agree there, and associativity shows that their meets agree there.
The identity therefore bounds each of
\((a\vee c)\mathbin{\triangle}(b\vee d)\) and
\((a\wedge c)\mathbin{\triangle}(b\wedge d)\) by
\(\neg e=(a\mathbin{\triangle}b)\vee(c\mathbin{\triangle}d)\in I\).
Also \((\neg a)\mathbin{\triangle}(\neg b)=a\mathbin{\triangle}b\).
Thus \(\sim_I\) respects every operation.

Replacement forms the set of equivalence classes. Congruence makes
\([a]_I\wedge[b]_I=[a\wedge b]_I\), and similarly the join and
complement, single-valued independently of representatives. Each Boolean
axiom descends by applying the quotient map to that axiom in \(B\).
For any finitely many classes used in an axiom one may use representatives
in an existential argument; a global selector for all classes is neither
defined nor needed. The map \(q\) is a homomorphism and is surjective
by the definition of the quotient set. Since
\(a\mathbin{\triangle}0_B=a\), its zero kernel is exactly \(I\).
And \([0_B]_I=[1_B]_I\) iff
\(0_B\mathbin{\triangle}1_B=1_B\in I\); nontriviality is therefore
equivalent to properness of \(I\).

If \(Q\) is a prime ideal of the quotient, let \(P=q^{-1}[Q]\).
It contains zero, excludes one, is closed under joins, and is downward
closed because homomorphisms preserve the Boolean order. If
\(a\wedge b\in P\), then \(q(a)\wedge q(b)\in Q\);
primeness gives \(q(a)\in Q\) or \(q(b)\in Q\), as required.
For \(i\in I\), \(q(i)=[0_B]_I\in Q\), so \(I\subseteq P\).
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p01-bpi-finite-local}{thm:p01-bpi-finite-local}{Finite local Boolean evaluations}
\begin{proof}
Fix the finite list. Distributing
\(\bigwedge_{k=1}^{n}(b_k\vee\neg b_k)=1_B\) gives
\(\bigvee_{\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^{n}}e_\varepsilon=1_B\).
If two indices differ in their \(k\)-th bit, the corresponding cells
have a meet containing \(b_k\wedge\neg b_k\), and hence have zero
meet. Discarding zero cells leaves a finite disjoint family with join one;
at least one survives since the algebra is nontrivial.

The joins of subfamilies of these cells form a subalgebra: joins take
unions of subfamilies, meets take intersections because the cells are
disjoint, and complement takes the remaining cells of the partition.
For the complement assertion, the selected and remaining joins have zero
meet and total join one, so uniqueness of complements gives the claim.
Each \(b_k\) is the join of cells whose \(k\)-th bit is one, by
distributing \(b_k\) against the other \(b_j\vee\neg b_j\).
Conversely every cell is a finite Boolean expression in the generators.
Thus the generated subalgebra is exactly this finite family of joins.
This is an algebraic distribution argument, not an application of Stone
representation or of prime-ideal existence.

Let \(E\subseteq I\) be finite and included among the generators.
The finite join \(j=\bigvee E\) lies in \(I\); since \(I\) is proper,
\(j\ne1_B\), so \(\neg j\ne0_B\). It belongs to the generated
subalgebra and is a join of cells. At least one cell in that join is
nonzero; fix such an \(e\). For any \(c\) in the subalgebra,
\(e\wedge c\) is either \(e\) or \(0_B\); hence precisely one of
\(e\leq_B c,e\leq_B\neg c\) holds. Meet and join of cell subfamilies
then show that \(h(c)=1\) iff \(e\leq_B c\) preserves both
operations, complements and constants. Every \(i\in E\) lies below
\(j\), while \(e\leq_B\neg j\), so \(e\wedge i=0_B\), and
\(h(i)=0\).

When \(n=0\), there is just the empty cell \(1_B\); the subalgebra
is \(\{0_B,1_B\}\). When \(E=\varnothing\), \(j=0_B\), and any
nonzero cell works. Fixing a witness for this one finite instance is an
existential inference in ZF; it is not simultaneous selection over the set
of all finite instances.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p01-bpi-equivalence}{thm:p01-bpi-equivalence}{BPI, Boolean extension, and set ultrafilters}
\begin{proof}
\emph{Bare BPI implies ideal extension.} Given a proper ideal \(I\) of
\(B\), the quotient lemma gives a nontrivial algebra \(B/I\).
Apply BPI there and pull its prime ideal back along \(q\). The lemma
proves that the resulting proper prime ideal contains \(I\).
Conversely, \(\{0_B\}\) is a proper ideal of every nontrivial
Boolean algebra, so ideal extension implies bare BPI.

\emph{Ideal extension is equivalent to Boolean filter extension.}
The dual of a proper filter \(F\) is a proper ideal \(d(F)\).
If \(P\supseteq d(F)\) is prime, its dual
\(U=d(P)=B\setminus P\) is an ultrafilter and contains \(F\),
by inclusion-preserving duality. Conversely the dual of a proper ideal
extends to an ultrafilter \(U\); its dual prime ideal \(d(U)\)
contains the original ideal. The duality lemma proves every assertion
used in these constructions.

\emph{Boolean filter extension implies the set Ultrafilter Lemma.}
Apply it to \(\mathcal P(S)\). Its ultrafilter decides precisely one
of \(A,S\setminus A\) for every \(A\subseteq S\), by the duality
lemma. This is exactly the inherited formulation. If \(S\) is empty,
no proper filter was given and the instance is vacuous.

\emph{The set Ultrafilter Lemma implies ideal extension on every algebra.}
Let \(I\) be a proper ideal in a Boolean algebra \(B\), so
\(B\) is nontrivial. Let \(X=\mathbf2^B\) be the set of all
functions \(v:B\to\mathbf2\), not initially homomorphisms.
The constant-zero function shows that \(X\) is nonempty without Choice.
For \(b\in B\), put \(T_b=\{v\in X:v(b)=1\}\).
Use the following subsets of \(X\) as constraints:
\[
\begin{aligned}
 C_0&=\{v:v(0_B)=0\},& C_1&=\{v:v(1_B)=1\},\\
 C^{\neg}_b&=\{v:v(\neg b)=\neg v(b)\},&&\\
 C^{\wedge}_{a,b}&=\{v:v(a\wedge b)=v(a)\wedge v(b)\},&&\\
 C^{\vee}_{a,b}&=\{v:v(a\vee b)=v(a)\vee v(b)\},&&\\
 C_i&=\{v:v(i)=0\}&&(i\in I).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here every \(v\) is restricted to \(X\), and the operations on its
values are in \(\mathbf2\). Their collection is a set by Replacement
and Separation.

Every finite collection of constraints has nonempty intersection.
For each of its finitely many members fix one of the displayed constraint
indices defining it; such finite witness selection is proved in ZF by
induction on the number of members. Then collect all Boolean elements
occurring in those constraints,
including the operation results and any mentioned \(i\in I\), into
a finite list, and let \(E\) be its finite ideal constraints. The
finite local lemma gives a homomorphism on the generated subalgebra
annihilating \(E\). Define \(v\) to equal that homomorphism on the
subalgebra and to be zero outside it. This is a total function specified
by two disjoint cases and satisfies each of the selected constraints.
The empty collection is satisfied by any member of \(X\).
The generated set filter of all constraints is therefore proper.
Use the set Ultrafilter Lemma once to extend it to \(\mathcal U\).

By the duality lemma, its characteristic function
\(\chi:\mathcal P(X)\to\mathbf2\) is a Boolean homomorphism.
Define \(h(b)=\chi(T_b)\). If \(C\in\mathcal U\) and
\(C\cap A=C\cap A'\), then
\(\chi(A)=\chi(C)\wedge\chi(A)=\chi(C\cap A)
=\chi(C\cap A')=\chi(A')\).
Since every constraint belongs to \(\mathcal U\), their pointwise
identities imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
 h(0_B)&=0,& h(1_B)&=1,\\
 h(\neg b)&=\neg h(b),& h(a\wedge b)&=h(a)\wedge h(b),\\
 h(a\vee b)&=h(a)\vee h(b),& h(i)&=0\quad(i\in I).
\end{aligned}
\]
For example, on \(C^{\wedge}_{a,b}\) the sets
\(T_{a\wedge b}\) and \(T_a\cap T_b\) coincide; apply the preceding
equality and the homomorphism law for \(\chi\). On \(C^{\neg}_b\),
\(T_{\neg b}\) coincides with \(X\setminus T_b\). On \(C_0,C_1,C_i\),
the corresponding cylinder is respectively empty, all of the constraint,
or empty. This verifies each equation rather than presupposing a limiting
valuation.

The zero kernel \(P=\{b:h(b)=0\}\) is a proper ideal: homomorphism
laws give the constants and join closure, and preserve order for downward
closure. If \(h(a\wedge b)=0\), the two-element truth table forces
\(h(a)=0\) or \(h(b)=0\), so \(P\) is prime. It contains \(I\).
Only this one application of the set Ultrafilter Lemma goes beyond ZF.
In particular, no well-order of \(B\), extension of finite homomorphisms
to all of \(B\), family of preselected finite witnesses, or Boolean
representation theorem has been used.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p01-bpi-propositional-compactness}{thm:p01-bpi-propositional-compactness}{The two compactness directions}
\begin{proof}
\emph{Ultrafilter extension implies compactness.} Let
\(\Gamma\) be finitely satisfiable over \(V\). The set
\(X=\mathbf2^V\) of total valuations is nonempty: if \(V\) is empty
its sole member is the empty function; otherwise the constant-zero
function is available. For a formula \(\varphi\), define its truth set
\(T_\varphi=\{v\in X:v(\varphi)=1\}\).
Structural recursion on finite formulas gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 T_\bot&=\varnothing,& T_\top&=X,\\
 T_{\neg\varphi}&=X\setminus T_\varphi,&&\\
 T_{\varphi\land\psi}&=T_\varphi\cap T_\psi,&&\\
 T_{\varphi\lor\psi}&=T_\varphi\cup T_\psi.&&
\end{aligned}
\]
Finite satisfiability means precisely that every finite intersection of
truth sets for members of \(\Gamma\) is nonempty. Therefore they
generate a proper set filter. Extend it to \(\mathcal U\) by the
set Ultrafilter Lemma and let \(\chi\) be its characteristic
homomorphism on \(\mathcal P(X)\). Define a valuation
\(\nu(v)=\chi(T_{p_v})\) for \(v\in V\). Its values form one
function by Replacement, not separate choices. Induction on formula
construction using the displayed identities and the homomorphism laws
gives \(\nu(\varphi)=\chi(T_\varphi)\): the variable case is the
definition, both constant cases use the constant laws, and each of
negation, conjunction and disjunction uses the corresponding law.
Every \(T_\gamma\) lies in \(\mathcal U\), so
\(\nu(\gamma)=1\) for every \(\gamma\in\Gamma\). This supplies
compactness. The equivalence theorem supplies the same implication
from BPI without importing AC.

\emph{Compactness implies Boolean ideal extension.} Let \(I\) be a
proper ideal of a nontrivial Boolean algebra \(B\). Introduce distinct
variables \(p_b\) for \(b\in B\), using tagged syntax if an element
of \(B\) already happens to be a formula. Take the following set of
finite formulas:
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \neg p_{0_B},\qquad p_{1_B},\qquad
 p_{\neg b}\Leftrightarrow\neg p_b,\\
 p_{a\wedge b}\Leftrightarrow(p_a\land p_b),\qquad
 p_{a\vee b}\Leftrightarrow(p_a\lor p_b),\qquad
 \neg p_i\quad(i\in I).
\end{gathered}
\]
Here \(\Leftrightarrow\) abbreviates the Boolean expression for equal
truth values; it is formula equivalence, not elementary equivalence of
structures. For any finite subset, collect all mentioned algebra
elements, including operation results, into a finite list. Apply the
finite local lemma to its ideal constraints and define a total assignment
to be its finite-subalgebra homomorphism there and zero on all other
elements. Every selected formula is then true. Thus the displayed set is
finitely satisfiable, and compactness gives a valuation satisfying all
of it. The function \(h(b)=\nu(p_b)\) consequently preserves every
Boolean operation and both constants, and annihilates \(I\). Its
zero kernel is a prime ideal containing \(I\), by the kernel argument
in the preceding annex item. The equivalence theorem completes all the
other implications.

Finally, this proof uses compactness for the variable set indexed by all
of \(B\), not just a countable subset. For a fixed enumerable alphabet,
the separate binary-tree argument of Part~6 uses its supplied enumeration
and the fixed order of the two bits and requires no ultrafilter principle.
The two assertions have different domains. Truth constants cause no
extra strength: for a nonempty variable set fix one variable \(p\)
and replace \(\top,\bot\) by \(p\lor\neg p,p\land\neg p\).
This translation preserves truth under every valuation. For an empty
alphabet the single empty valuation evaluates every constants-only
formula; finite satisfiability already excludes any false formula by
testing its singleton. Thus the constants convention does not hide a
choice assumption or a failed empty-alphabet case.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p01-bpi-ac-implication}{thm:p01-bpi-ac-implication}{The precise Zorn application}
\begin{proof}
Assume AC and fix a proper Boolean filter \(F\subseteq B\).
The set
\(\mathcal Q=\{G\subseteq B:G\text{ is a proper filter and }F\subseteq G\}\)
exists by Separation from \(\mathcal P(B)\) and is nonempty because it
contains \(F\). Order it by inclusion. A nonempty chain
\(\mathcal C\) has upper bound \(G_*=\bigcup\mathcal C\): it
contains \(F\) and \(1_B\), excludes \(0_B\), and is upward closed.
If \(a,b\in G_*\), they belong to two members of the chain, and
one of those contains the other. Both elements and their meet therefore
belong to that larger filter and hence to \(G_*\). It is a proper
filter. The empty chain has the upper bound \(F\), so the hypothesis
including empty chains is satisfied. The Choice-to-Zorn theorem of Part~6
now gives a maximal \(U\in\mathcal Q\). Any proper filter extending
\(U\) still contains \(F\), so maximality in \(\mathcal Q\)
is maximality among all proper Boolean filters. Thus \(U\) is an
ultrafilter. The ZF equivalence already proved gives BPI.
The only non-ZF premise in this argument is Zorn supplied by AC; the
chain union and all earlier algebraic constructions use ZF alone.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p01-bpi-set-boundaries}{thm:p01-bpi-set-boundaries}{Finite and cofinite filters}
\begin{proof}
For any set \(S\), if an ultrafilter is generated by a single
\(A\subseteq S\), properness gives \(A\ne\varnothing\). Fix
\(s\in A\). If \(A\ne\{s\}\), then neither \(\{s\}\) nor
\(S\setminus\{s\}\) contains \(A\), so neither is in the
generated filter, contradicting ultrafilter decision. Thus \(A=\{s\}\),
and the filter is \(U_s\). Conversely every point filter is generated
by its singleton and is an ultrafilter by decision. This verifies the
equivalence of the two principal-ultrafilter conventions.

Suppose \(S\) is finite and \(F\) is a proper filter on it.
Then \(S\ne\varnothing\) and \(\mathcal P(S)\), hence \(F\),
is finite in ZF. These finite-set facts follow by induction on a finite
enumeration of \(S\): adjoining one point doubles the power-set list,
and a subset of a finite list has a finite list. The intersection
\(A=\bigcap F\) is therefore a finite intersection of members of
\(F\), belongs to \(F\), and is nonempty by properness. Fix one
\(s\in A\). Then \(U_s=\{Y\subseteq S:s\in Y\}\) is a proper
filter deciding every subset by whether it contains \(s\), hence an
ultrafilter, and it contains \(F\). Selecting this single witness is
not an axiom of simultaneous choice for a family.

If \(U\) is any ultrafilter on finite \(S\), the same finite
intersection argument gives a point \(s\in\bigcap U\) and
\(U\subseteq U_s\). Maximality gives equality. More directly,
primeness applied repeatedly to the finite union of singletons making
\(S\) gives a singleton in \(U\); two distinct singletons cannot
both belong to a proper filter. Thus the principal point is unique.

Now let \(S\) be infinite, meaning not finite, without assuming a
countably infinite subset. Its cofinite family
\(F_{\mathrm{cof}}=\{Y\subseteq S:S\setminus Y\text{ is finite}\}\)
contains \(S\) and excludes \(\varnothing\). It is upward closed
because a subset of a finite set is finite. It is meet closed because
the union of two finite complements is finite, a fact proved by
concatenating finite lists and deleting repetitions. Therefore it is
a proper filter in ZF. Assuming BPI, the equivalence theorem extends it
to an ultrafilter \(U\). If \(T\subseteq S\) is finite, then
\(S\setminus T\in F_{\mathrm{cof}}\subseteq U\), so
\(T\notin U\), since the two have empty intersection. In particular
no singleton belongs to \(U\), while \(U_s\) contains \(\{s\}\)
for every \(s\in S\). Thus \(U\) is not principal. The extra
existence step is exactly ultrafilter extension, not a purported ZF
construction of a free ultrafilter.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p02.fbc.finite-syntax}{thm:p02-fbc-finite-syntax}{Finite support, nonvacuous discharge, and finite schemata}
\begin{proof}
A derivation is a finite tree, so it has finitely many leaves and hence
finitely many open assumption formulas. The same tree is permitted
whenever its finite open set is contained in the stated premise set.
This proves monotonicity and finite support without a weakening rule.

For padding, take the given derivation of \(\beta\), add a fresh
assumption leaf \(\alpha\), apply \(\land I\) to obtain
\(\beta\land\alpha\), and apply \(\land E_1\) to conclude \(\beta\).
The new leaf remains an actual open occurrence.
If a derivation of \(\beta\) from \(\Gamma\cup\{\alpha\}\) has
open \(\alpha\)-occurrences, mark all of them with one label fresh
from every existing label, using the source merging operation.
No old discharge uses that fresh label, so those occurrences stay open
until the new root \(\to I\), which discharges them all.
All remaining open formulas belong to \(\Gamma\).
If none occurs, the original derivation is already from \(\Gamma\);
perform the padding just described and discharge its new leaf instead.
In either case the discharge is nonvacuous.
For the reverse implication, take a fresh-labelled copy of the
derivation of \(\alpha\to\beta\), add an assumption \(\alpha\),
and apply \(\to E\). The resulting open set is contained in
\(\Gamma\cup\{\alpha\}\).

Uniform formula substitution fixes \(\bottom\) and commutes with
each primitive constructor. Apply it to the formula at every node
of a finite derivation, leaving matching assumption/rule labels intact.
Each assumption is still an assumption; each \(\land I,\land E\),
\(\lor I,\lor E,\to I,\to E,\neg I,\neg E,\bottom E\) and RAA
instance is the same rule with its formula metavariables substituted.
Every discharged labelled occurrence is still present and has the
substituted bracketed formula. Thus no discharge becomes vacuous,
even if different old formulas obtain equal substitutions.
Substitution does not act again inside an inserted formula.
When copies are assembled, finitely many labels can be renamed to
distinct natural numbers greater than every receiving label.
This is a finite construction, not a choice of names across an
arbitrary family.

Now take a tautological schema \(\theta(p_0,\ldots,p_{k-1})\) in
the fixed source alphabet. Its truth value depends only on these
finitely many atoms, by structural induction. Validity for their
binary assignments therefore makes it valid for all assignments on
the source countable alphabet. The already proved
\cref{thm:prop-completeness}, with empty premise set, gives a closed
finite derivation of \(\theta\). That theorem's actual proof uses
the source countable Lindenbaum enumeration and truth lemma,
not Boolean quotients or arbitrary-language completeness.
That enumeration requires no Choice: encode \(p_n\) by its
natural-number binary digits with fixed delimiters, encode the
finitely many other tokens by fixed characters, and enumerate the
resulting finite words by length and then lexicographically.
Retaining the well-formed encodings lists every source formula.
This construction concerns the given indexed source atoms, not \(P\).
Assign prescribed \(P\)-formulas to the displayed \(k\) atoms and
\(\bottom\) to every unused source atom. This explicitly defines
one total substitution even when \(P=\varnothing\).
The preceding rule induction gives the desired closed instance.
Only this one proof of the selected schema is used; no simultaneous
selection of proofs for all schemata is stipulated.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p02.fbc.boolean-soundness}{thm:p02-fbc-boolean-soundness}{Boolean-valued soundness for every ND rule}
\begin{proof}
The complement/order calculus of \cref{thm:p01-bpi-duality} follows
from Boolean axioms and uses no representation or choice.
In particular
\[
 r\wedge s=0_B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r\leq_B\neg s.
\]
We will also use the residuation identity
\[
 x\wedge a\leq_B b
       \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\leq_B\neg a\vee b.
\]
For the forward direction distribute
\(x=x\wedge(a\vee\neg a)\):
the first summand is below \(b\), the second below \(\neg a\).
For the reverse direction meet \(x\leq_B\neg a\vee b\) with \(a\);
the upper bound becomes \(a\wedge b\leq_B b\).
These calculations remain valid when \(0_B=1_B\).

Induct on the derivation, using the meet of its actual finite open
assumption values, not of the possibly infinite permitted set.
An assumption leaf has value \(a\) and open meet \(a\).
For \(\land I\), if the premise meets are \(x,y\), then
\(x\leq a\), \(y\leq b\) imply \(x\wedge y\leq a\wedge b\).
Overlapping open sets cause no problem, since repeats are idempotent.
For \(\land E_1,\land E_2\), the premise bound
\(x\leq a\wedge b\) implies the respective bound to \(a,b\).
For \(\lor I_1,\lor I_2\), use respectively
\(a\leq a\vee b\) and \(b\leq a\vee b\).

For \(\to E\), the combined open meet is below both
\(\neg a\vee b\) and \(a\), hence below
\(a\wedge(\neg a\vee b)=a\wedge b\leq b\).
For \(\neg E\), it is below \(a\wedge\neg a=0_B\).
For \(\bottom E\), a bound below \(0_B\) is below every element.

For \(\to I\), let \(x\) be the meet of remaining open
assumptions and \(a\) the value of the discharged formula.
The premise open meet is \(x\wedge a\), even if some
undischarged occurrences of the same formula remain in \(x\).
The induction hypothesis gives \(x\wedge a\leq b\);
residuation gives \(x\leq\neg a\vee b\).
For \(\neg I\), it gives \(x\wedge a\leq0_B\), hence
\(x\leq\neg a\).
For RAA the discharged formula has value \(\neg a\);
the premise gives \(x\wedge\neg a\leq0_B\), hence
\(x\leq\neg\neg a=a\).
This is exactly where Boolean, rather than merely intuitionistic,
complementation supports the classical rule.

For \(\lor E\), let the major premise meet be \(x\) and let
the subsidiary remaining-open meets be \(y,z\).
With \(a,b\) the disjunct values and \(c\) the conclusion value,
the induction hypotheses are
\[
 x\leq a\vee b,\qquad y\wedge a\leq c,\qquad
 z\wedge b\leq c.
\]
The final open meet \(x\wedge y\wedge z\) is below
\[
 (a\vee b)\wedge y\wedge z
       =(a\wedge y\wedge z)\vee(b\wedge y\wedge z)
       \leq c.
\]
Both labelled branch assumptions are accounted for before removal.
These cases exhaust the actual rule sheet.

A closed tree has empty open meet \(1_B\), so its conclusion value
is \(1_B\). If that conclusion is \(\alpha\leftrightarrow\beta\),
both \(\neg a\vee b\) and \(\neg b\vee a\) are one.
Residuation with \(x=1_B\) gives \(a\leq b\) and \(b\leq a\),
hence \(a=b\). No completeness assertion was used.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p02.fbc.quotient}{thm:p02-fbc-quotient}{Congruence and all Boolean identities of the syntactic quotient}
\begin{proof}
The value of a biconditional in \(\mathbf2\) is one exactly when
its two arguments have equal values. Thus the following finite schemata
are tautologies: \(\alpha\leftrightarrow\alpha\);
\((\alpha\leftrightarrow\beta)\to(\beta\leftrightarrow\alpha)\);
and
\[
 ((\alpha\leftrightarrow\beta)\land
   (\beta\leftrightarrow\gamma))
       \to(\alpha\leftrightarrow\gamma).
\]
The first is equality with itself, the second reverses equality,
and the third is transitivity of equal binary values.
\Cref{thm:p02-fbc-finite-syntax} gives closed ND instances.
Conjunction introduction and implication elimination on the given
closed equivalences establish reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity
of \(\sim_P\).

For congruence, the finite schema
\[
 (\alpha\leftrightarrow\alpha')
                 \to(\neg\alpha\leftrightarrow\neg\alpha')
\]
is tautological, since complementation is a function on binary values.
For each \(\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to\}\), so is
\[
 ((\alpha\leftrightarrow\alpha')\land
   (\beta\leftrightarrow\beta'))
       \to((\alpha\circ\beta)\leftrightarrow
                              (\alpha'\circ\beta')).
\]
Equal pairs of inputs have equal outputs under each truth function.
Closed instances and \(\land I,\to E\) give all congruence clauses.

For explicitness, all the required Boolean identities are obtained
as biconditionals of the following formula pairs:
\[
\begin{array}{c}
 \alpha\land\beta,\ \beta\land\alpha\\
 \alpha\lor\beta,\ \beta\lor\alpha\\
 (\alpha\land\beta)\land\gamma,\ \alpha\land(\beta\land\gamma)\\
 (\alpha\lor\beta)\lor\gamma,\ \alpha\lor(\beta\lor\gamma)\\
 \alpha\land\alpha,\ \alpha\qquad
       \alpha\lor\alpha,\ \alpha\\
 \alpha\land(\alpha\lor\beta),\ \alpha\\
 \alpha\lor(\alpha\land\beta),\ \alpha\\
 \alpha\land\topv,\ \alpha\qquad\alpha\lor\bottom,\ \alpha\\
 \alpha\land\bottom,\ \bottom\qquad\alpha\lor\topv,\ \topv\\
 \alpha\land(\beta\lor\gamma),\
       (\alpha\land\beta)\lor(\alpha\land\gamma)\\
 \alpha\lor(\beta\land\gamma),\
       (\alpha\lor\beta)\land(\alpha\lor\gamma)\\
 \alpha\land\neg\alpha,\ \bottom\qquad
       \alpha\lor\neg\alpha,\ \topv\\
 \neg\neg\alpha,\ \alpha\\
 \alpha\to\beta,\ \neg\alpha\lor\beta\\
 \neg(\alpha\land\beta),\ \neg\alpha\lor\neg\beta\\
 \neg(\alpha\lor\beta),\ \neg\alpha\land\neg\beta .
\end{array}
\]
Here commas separate the two members of a pair, not premises.
We verify that every pair has equal binary values before invoking
finite schematic derivability.
In \(\mathbf2\), conjunction is minimum and disjunction is maximum.
Commutativity follows because exchanging the two inputs does not
change their lower or upper value. Both associations give the least
or greatest of the same three inputs. Idempotence uses one input twice.
For absorption, \(u\leq\max(u,v)\) and \(\min(u,v)\leq u\);
the indicated outer minimum or maximum is consequently \(u\).
The four bound laws follow from \(0\leq u\leq1\).
For meet distributing over join, \(u=0\) makes both sides zero;
\(u=1\) makes both sides \(\max(v,w)\).
For the dual distribution, \(u=1\) makes both sides one;
\(u=0\) makes both sides \(\min(v,w)\).
For \(u=0\), the complement is one; for \(u=1\), it is zero.
In both cases their minimum is zero and their maximum is one.
Double negation is \(1-(1-u)=u\).
For the complement of a meet, the two sides have value one when
both inputs are zero, zero when both are one, and one when they differ.
For the complement of a join, those three cases give respectively
one, zero and zero on both sides. These exhaust the four assignments.
The implication pair is its specified binary truth table:
when \(u=0\) both sides are one, and when \(u=1\) both equal \(v\).
Each biconditional is therefore tautological, and
\cref{thm:p02-fbc-finite-syntax} gives its closed proof.

Replacement forms the set of all equivalence classes.
Congruence makes each displayed operation a well-defined function:
any two representatives of one input have equivalent outputs, and
the same holds for the two inputs of a binary operation.
Representatives of the finitely many classes in a particular identity
exist by finite witness selection in ZF; no selector on all classes
is required. The closed biconditionals just proved show that each
listed identity holds in the quotient. They include every bounded
distributive lattice and complement axiom, making it a Boolean algebra.
The last implication pair gives the asserted implication interpretation.

Finally a total valuation on \(P\) exists without Choice: assign
zero to every atom, using the empty function when \(P\) is empty.
Its recursive extension sends \(\bottom\) to zero and
\(\topv=\neg\bottom\) to one. If their classes were equal,
Boolean-valued soundness in \(\mathbf2\) would make these values equal,
which is false. Thus \(L_P\) is nontrivial in every case.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p02.fbc.free}{thm:p02-fbc-free}{The universal map and syntactic order}
\begin{proof}
Fix a Boolean algebra \(B\) and an assignment \(f:P\to B\).
Structural recursion on finite formulas defines
\(\llbracket\alpha\rrbracket_f\).
If \(\alpha\sim_P\beta\), the given closed proof of their
biconditional and \cref{thm:p02-fbc-boolean-soundness} give equal
values. The relation
\[
 h_f([\alpha]_P)=\llbracket\alpha\rrbracket_f
\]
therefore specifies exactly one value at every class, independently
of all its representatives. Replacement forms its graph as a function;
it does not choose a representative for each class.
The evaluation clauses preserve zero, one, complement, meet and join,
and on an atomic class give \(h_f([p]_P)=f(p)\).
Thus \(h_f\) is a homomorphism with \(h_f\eta_P=f\).

If \(h\) is any such homomorphism, induction on \(\alpha\) gives
\(h([\alpha]_P)=\llbracket\alpha\rrbracket_f\).
The atomic case is \(h\eta_P=f\); the bottom case is preservation
of zero. Negation, meet and join use their quotient definitions and
homomorphism laws. Implication uses the already established identity
\([\alpha\to\beta]=\neg[\alpha]\vee[\beta]\).
These exhaust the grammar, proving uniqueness.
No nontriviality of \(B\) was required. If it is trivial all values
and all the preservation equations still exist and agree.

For distinct atoms \(p,q\), the assignment to \(\mathbf2\) taking
value one precisely at \(p\) and zero at every other atom is a set
function defined by Separation. Its induced homomorphism sends
\([p]\) to one and \([q]\) to zero, so those classes differ.
Hence \(\eta_P\) is injective.
If \(P=\varnothing\), induction on a formula shows that its class
is either \(0_L\) or \(1_L\): bottom starts at zero; complement
interchanges zero and one; meet and join of these two stay among them;
and implication is complement followed by join.
Their distinctness was proved in the quotient item.
The same existence/uniqueness proof applies to the sole empty assignment
into any target algebra.

For the order assertion, the two finite schemata
\[
 ((\alpha\land\beta)\leftrightarrow\alpha)\to(\alpha\to\beta),
 \qquad
 (\alpha\to\beta)\to((\alpha\land\beta)\leftrightarrow\alpha)
\]
are tautological. Indeed \(\min(u,v)=u\) iff \(u=0\) or \(v=1\),
and that is exactly the condition for \(u\to v=1\).
Their closed instances exist by finite schematic derivability.
The equation \([\alpha]\wedge[\beta]=[\alpha]\) is, by the
quotient definition, the existence of the first inner biconditional
as a closed proof. Modus ponens with the first schema gives
\(\varnothing\vdash_P\alpha\to\beta\).
Conversely that closed implication and the second schema give
the biconditional and hence the defining order equation.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p02.fbc.filter}{thm:p02-fbc-filter}{The exact premise-filter correspondence}
\begin{proof}
The empty sequence shows \(1_L\in F_\Gamma\), and a one-member
sequence shows \([\gamma]\in F_\Gamma\) for each \(\gamma\in\Gamma\).
Transitivity of order proves upward closure.
Concatenating two witnessing finite sequences gives a meet below the
meet of their respective upper bounds, so proves meet closure.
Every filter containing the generators contains each finite meet and
everything above it. Thus \(F_\Gamma\) is exactly their least filter,
also the generated filter of \cref{thm:p01-bpi-duality}.

For the forward derivability-to-membership implication, interpret the
calculus in \(L_P\) by the assignment \(p\mapsto[p]_P\).
Induction on a formula gives
\(\llbracket\alpha\rrbracket_\eta=[\alpha]_P\): the bottom,
complement, meet and join cases are definitions, and the implication
case uses its proved quotient identity.
If \(D\) derives \(\varphi\) with open formulas in \(\Gamma\),
Boolean-valued soundness gives
\[
 \bigwedge_{\delta\in\operatorname{oa}(D)}[\delta]_P
                                  \leq_L[\varphi]_P .
\]
Its finite open set can be listed in a finite sequence in ZF;
this one sequence witnesses membership.

Conversely take a witnessing finite sequence
\(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n\), and let \(\tau\) be its
right-associated formula conjunction.
Its class is the witnessing Boolean meet, including
\([\tau]=[\topv]=1_L\) when \(n=0\).
The inequality to \([\varphi]\) and the syntactic order theorem
give a closed proof of \(\tau\to\varphi\).
For \(n>0\), fresh assumption leaves for the sequence entries and
successive \(\land I\) from the right build \(\tau\).
If entries repeat, distinct labelled leaves are allowed; their
permitted formula set is still contained in \(\Gamma\).
For \(n=0\), assume \(\bottom\) as one fresh leaf and discharge
that very leaf by \(\neg I\); this gives the closed proof
of \(\neg\bottom=\topv=\tau\).
Freshen the labels of the closed implication proof and apply
\(\to E\) to these two derivations.
No extra assumption is introduced; the resulting open set is
contained in the finite sequence's members, and hence in \(\Gamma\).
This proves the reverse correspondence with actual ND trees.

Taking \(\varphi=\bottom\) shows that inconsistency is equivalent
to \(0_L\in F_\Gamma\). A filter containing zero contains every
element by upward closure; conversely the whole algebra contains zero.
Thus properness is exactly consistency.
When \(\Gamma=\varnothing\), only the empty sequence is permitted,
so its upper bounds are exactly \(1_L\), proving
\(F_\varnothing=\{1_L\}\). Nontriviality makes this filter proper.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p02.fbc.separation}{thm:p02-fbc-separation}{The avoiding filter and every truth-lemma constructor}
\begin{proof}
Write \(F=F_\Gamma\) and \(a=[\varphi]_P\).
The correspondence gives \(a\notin F\); this also implies \(F\)
proper, since an improper filter contains everything.
The displayed \(H\) contains one by witness \(f=1_L\), and contains
\(\neg a\) by the same witness. Every \(f\in F\) belongs to \(H\),
since \(f\wedge\neg a\leq f\).
It is upward closed. If \(b,c\) have witnesses \(f,g\in F\),
then \(f\wedge g\in F\) and
\[
 (f\wedge g)\wedge\neg a
        =(f\wedge\neg a)\wedge(g\wedge\neg a)\leq b\wedge c .
\]
Thus \(H\) is a filter.
If it contained zero, some \(f\in F\) would satisfy
\(f\wedge\neg a=0_L\), hence \(f\leq a\) by Boolean
complement/order calculus. Upward closure would put \(a\) in \(F\),
contrary to the premise. This proves properness before extension.

Assume BPI and use \cref{thm:p01-bpi-equivalence} once to extend
this prescribed proper filter to an ultrafilter \(U\).
Since \(\neg a\in U\), properness forbids \(a\in U\).
The ZF duality theorem \cref{thm:p01-bpi-duality} proves that
\(\chi_U:L_P\to\mathbf2\) preserves both constants and all
Boolean operations. Define \(v_U=\chi_U\eta_P\).
This is one specified function on \(P\), not separate choices
of a truth value for each atom.

Induct on the formula for the truth lemma.
For an atom it is the definition.
For bottom, both sides are zero by preservation of \(0_L\).
For negation, both sides are the Boolean complement of the value
of the immediate subformula, by the induction hypothesis and
preservation of complement.
For conjunction and disjunction, use the corresponding two
induction hypotheses and preservation of meet and join.
For implication, use
\[
 \chi_U([\alpha\to\beta])
     =\chi_U(\neg[\alpha]\vee[\beta])
     =\neg\chi_U([\alpha])\vee\chi_U([\beta]),
\]
which is precisely its recursive binary truth value.
The defined \(\topv\) case follows from negation of bottom.
These are all primitive constructors and no infinitary clause
is introduced.
For \(\gamma\in\Gamma\), its class belongs to \(F\subseteq U\)
and so its truth value is one. The class \(a\) is excluded,
so \(\varphi\) has value zero.
The proof includes empty \(\Gamma\) and empty \(P\);
if the latter occurs, \(v_U\) is the unique empty assignment.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p02.fbc.completeness}{thm:p02-fbc-completeness}{Completeness, finite support and equivalence to BPI}
\begin{proof}
For soundness take \(B=\mathbf2\) in Boolean-valued soundness.
A valuation satisfying all permitted premises gives value one
to the finite open meet, hence to the conclusion.
This works in ZF alone.

Assume BPI. If \(\Gamma\not\vdash_P\varphi\), the preceding
construction gives a total valuation satisfying \(\Gamma\) and
falsifying \(\varphi\). This is exactly
\(\Gamma\not\models_P\varphi\); contraposition gives completeness.
When \(\Gamma\models_P\varphi\), its obtained derivation has
finite open set \(\Gamma_0\subseteq\Gamma\).
The same derivation is from \(\Gamma_0\), and soundness gives
\(\Gamma_0\models_P\varphi\).

If every finite subset of \(\Gamma\) is satisfiable but
\(\Gamma\) has no satisfying valuation, then
\(\Gamma\models_P\bottom\).
Completeness gives a finite derivation of bottom, and its finite
open set \(\Gamma_0\) cannot be satisfiable by soundness.
This contradicts the premise. The converse follows by using any
model of \(\Gamma\) for each subset.

For the choice-strength converse, assume over ZF the completeness
scheme for every set \(P\), without initially assuming BPI.
The same bottom/finite-support argument, now using that scheme
and the already choice-free soundness lemma, proves compactness
for every such \(P\).
Restrict to the \(\neg,\land,\lor\) fragment and interpret the
separate top constant of
\cref{def:p01-bpi-propositional-compactness} by the source
abbreviation \(\neg\bottom\).
Induction on formulas shows that this translation preserves every
truth value. It also covers the empty atom set, since no atom
is needed to form either constant.
More explicitly, translate a finitely satisfiable set \(\Sigma\)
in the P1 language. For a finite subset of its translated image,
fix one preimage per member; this is finite witness selection in ZF.
Those finitely many preimages have a common valuation, which satisfies
the selected translated formulas by truth preservation.
The image is therefore finitely satisfiable. The compactness just
obtained supplies a valuation of the whole image; truth preservation
then makes it a valuation of every member of \(\Sigma\).
Thus we obtain exactly the arbitrary-set-variable compactness
principle, not merely its countable restriction.
The complete converse construction of
\cref{thm:p01-bpi-propositional-compactness} then gives BPI.
Together with the proved BPI-to-completeness direction this
establishes the scheme equivalence over ZF.

No unrestricted completeness was used in the quotient or free
property proof. The countable source theorem was used only for
closed finite schemata before those constructions, and its
independent enumeration proof remains within its fixed alphabet.
Nothing here makes a general algorithm or well-order for an
arbitrary set of atoms; the precise algorithmic boundary is proved in
\cref{thm:p02-w02-p02-017-no-coding,thm:p02-w02-p02-017-bpi-boundary}.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\section{Proofs for finite-input decision procedures and the arbitrary-language scope}
\label{sec:annex-p02-w02-p02-017-finite-input-scope}

Throughout, \(P\) is a set of atoms, tagged as in
\cref{def:p02-fbc-language}, and for \(Q\subseteq P\) the language
\(\operatorname{Form}(Q)\) is identified with the set of
\(\alpha\in\operatorname{Form}(P)\) satisfying
\(\operatorname{Var}(\alpha)\subseteq Q\).  Valuations take values in
\(\{0,1\}\).

\emph{Computability facts used.}  By \cref{thm:p04-tm-partial-recursive}
the computable functions of \cref{def:partial-computable} are exactly
the total partial recursive functions of \cref{def:p04-partial-recursive}.
That class is closed under composition and primitive recursion, and it
contains every primitive recursive function, as
the theorem of \cref{sec:turing-machines-02} also states.  The following
functions are primitive recursive, by the displayed recursions from
zero, successor, projections, addition and multiplication
(the example in \cref{sec:turing-machines-02}):
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \operatorname{pd}(0)=0,\quad \operatorname{pd}(n+1)=n;\qquad
 a\mathbin{\dot{-}}0=a,\quad a\mathbin{\dot{-}}(b+1)=\operatorname{pd}(a\mathbin{\dot{-}} b);\\
 \overline{\operatorname{sg}}(0)=1,\quad
 \overline{\operatorname{sg}}(n+1)=0;\qquad
 \operatorname{eq}(a,b)=\overline{\operatorname{sg}}
   \bigl((a\mathbin{\dot{-}} b)+(b\mathbin{\dot{-}} a)\bigr);\qquad
 \max(a,b)=a+(b\mathbin{\dot{-}} a).
\end{gathered}
\]
Thus \(\operatorname{eq}(a,b)=1\) iff \(a=b\), and otherwise
\(\operatorname{eq}(a,b)=0\).  A machine that transforms its input string
and halts may be followed by a second such machine: rename the second
machine's states apart, return the head to cell \(0\), and identify the
first machine's accepting state with the second machine's start state.
The encoding paragraph of \cref{sec:turing-machines-01} supplies halting machines for writing
\(\operatorname{bin}(m)\) and for reading a binary word as a number, and
\cref{def:p02-sat-taut} supplies the encoding of a formula string as a
terminating linear-time transformation.  Writing a fixed list of
characters before and after a given string is likewise a halting
transformation.

\emph{Size of code numbers.}  If \(\alpha\in\operatorname{Form}(P_{\N})\) contains the
variable \(p_m\), then the encoding of \(\alpha\) contains the binary
digits of \(m\), so the binary numeral of \(\ulcorner\alpha\urcorner\) has
more than \(\abs{\operatorname{bin}(m)}\) digits.  A number whose numeral
has \(L\) digits is at least \(2^{L-1}\), and
\(m<2^{\abs{\operatorname{bin}(m)}}\) for every \(m\), including
\(m=0\).  Hence
\begin{equation}
 \ulcorner\alpha\urcorner>m
 \qquad\text{whenever }p_m\text{ occurs in }\alpha .
 \tag{S1}
\end{equation}

\emph{A decidable witness relation for \(K\).}  The two proofs of
\cref{sec:p02-w02-p02-017-infinite-premises} share the following
construction.  By \cref{thm:universal-computation} the universal function, written
\(U(e,x)\) there and not to be confused with the output function
\(\mathsf U\) below, is partial computable, hence partial recursive by
\cref{thm:p04-tm-partial-recursive}.  The function
\(F(x)\simeq U(x,x)\simeq\varphi_x(x)\) is its composition with two
projections, hence partial recursive; here \(\varphi_x\) is the
partial function with index \(x\) in the program numbering of
\cref{sec:universal-reductions-01},
not a formula.  The normal form
\cref{thm:p04-kleene-normal-form} with \(k=1\) gives an index \(e^{*}\)
such that
\[
 F(x)\simeq\mathsf U\bigl(\mu y\,\mathsf T_1(e^{*},x,y)\bigr)
 \qquad(x\in\N).
\]
Write \(T(x,y)\) for \(\mathsf T_1(e^{*},x,y)\).  Its characteristic
function is the composition of the primitive recursive characteristic
function of \(\mathsf T_1\) with a constant and projections, so \(T\) is
decidable.  The minimization is defined exactly when some \(y\) satisfies
\(T(x,y)\), and it then returns the least such \(y\).  Therefore
\begin{equation}
 x\in K
 \iff \varphi_x(x)\text{ is defined}
 \iff F(x)\text{ is defined}
 \iff \exists y\,T(x,y).
 \tag{S2}
\end{equation}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p02-w02-p02-017-finite-reduction}{thm:p02-w02-p02-017-finite-reduction}{Finite inputs over an arbitrary set of atoms}
\begin{proof}
\emph{Clause 1.}  Induct on \(\alpha\).  For an atom \(q\),
\(\operatorname{Var}(q)=\{q\}\) and \(\widehat v(q)=v(q)=w(q)=\widehat
w(q)\).  For \(\bottom\) both values are \(0\).  Since
\(\operatorname{Var}(\neg\alpha)=\operatorname{Var}(\alpha)\) and
\(\operatorname{Var}(\alpha\circ\beta)=\operatorname{Var}(\alpha)\cup
\operatorname{Var}(\beta)\), agreement on the larger set gives agreement
on each immediate subformula; the induction hypotheses and the common
truth clause give equal values.

\emph{Clause 2.}  The valuation \(s^{0}\) is defined by cases on the
membership \(q\in A\); no choice is involved.  If some valuation \(v\)
satisfies \(\Gamma_0\), let \(s\) be the restriction of \(v\) to \(A\).
Then \(s^{0}\) agrees
with \(v\) on \(A\supseteq\operatorname{Var}(\gamma)\) for every
\(\gamma\in\Gamma_0\), so by clause~1 \(s^{0}\) satisfies \(\Gamma_0\).
The converse is immediate.  In the same way, if a valuation \(v\)
satisfies \(\Gamma_0\) and gives \(\varphi\) value \(0\), then
\(s^{0}\) does the same for that restriction \(s\), because
\(\operatorname{Var}(\varphi)\subseteq A\); so
\(\Gamma_0\not\models_P\varphi\) iff some \(s^{0}\) is a
countervaluation.  For finite \(A\), induction on \(\abs A\) shows that
there are exactly \(2^{\abs A}\) functions \(A\to\{0,1\}\); when
\(A=\varnothing\) the only one is the empty function and \(s^{0}\) is
the constant \(0\) valuation.

\emph{Clause 3.}  Induct on \(\alpha\in\operatorname{Form}(Q)\).  For an
atom \(q\in Q\), \(\widehat u(q^{c})=u(p_{c(q)})=v(q)=\widehat v(q)\).
For \(\bottom\) both values are \(0\).  The translation commutes with
\(\neg,\land,\lor,\to\), and both recursive truth definitions use the
same clauses, so the induction hypotheses carry over.  Given \(v\) on
\(P\), define \(u(p_n)=v(q)\) when \(n=c(q)\) for some \(q\in Q\), and
\(u(p_n)=0\) otherwise; injectivity of \(c\) makes the \(q\) unique, so
\(u\) is a single defined function.  Given \(u\) on \(P_{\N}\), define
\(v(q)=u(p_{c(q)})\) for \(q\in Q\) and \(v(q)=0\) for
\(q\in P\setminus Q\).  In both directions the partners satisfy the
hypothesis.  If \(v\) satisfies \(\Delta\), its partner \(u\) satisfies
\(\Delta^{c}\); if \(u\) satisfies \(\Delta^{c}\), its partner \(v\)
satisfies \(\Delta\).  For \(\Delta\cup\{\psi\}\subseteq
\operatorname{Form}(Q)\), a countervaluation to \(\Delta\models_P\psi\)
yields one to \(\Delta^{c}\models_{P_{\N}}\psi^{c}\) and conversely, by the same
partners.

\emph{Clause 4.}  Since \(A\) is finite there is a bijection
\(A\to\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), which is an atom coding of \(A\).  Fix any atom
coding \(c\) of \(A\).  By clause~3 with \(Q=A\), \(\Gamma_0\) is
satisfiable iff \(\Gamma_0^{c}\) is, and \(\Gamma_0\models_P\varphi\) iff
\(\Gamma_0^{c}\models_{P_{\N}}\varphi^{c}\).  The algorithm of
\cref{thm:p02-decidability} decides finite entailment for its encoded
inputs, and a finite set is satisfiable iff it does not entail
\(\bottom\).  Its answers on the encoded input over \(c\) are therefore
the truth values of statements about \(\Gamma_0\) and \(\varphi\) in
which \(c\) does not occur, so they coincide for all atom codings of
\(A\).  None of the clauses uses a choice principle or compactness.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p02-w02-p02-017-no-coding}{thm:p02-w02-p02-017-no-coding}{Only countable well-orderable atom sets can be coded}
\begin{proof}
Let \(c:P\to\N\) be injective.  Put \(a\prec b\) iff \(c(a)<c(b)\).  This
is a strict linear order because \(<\) is one and \(c\) is injective.  If
\(S\subseteq P\) is nonempty, \(c[S]\) has a least element \(m\), and the
unique \(a\in S\) with \(c(a)=m\) is \(\prec\)-least in \(S\).  So
\(\prec\) well-orders \(P\), and \(c\) is the required injection into
\(\N\).

Let \(C:\operatorname{Form}(P)\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) be injective.  The map
\(q\mapsto q\), sending an atom to the atomic formula, is injective, and
so is \(\nu:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\N\) sending \(w\) to the number whose binary
numeral is \(1w\): the numeral of a positive number has no leading zero,
and deleting its first digit recovers \(w\).  The composite
\(q\mapsto\nu(C(q))\) is an atom coding, and the first paragraph applies.

If \(g:\mathcal P(\N)\to\N\) were injective, the map sending \(n\) to
\(g^{-1}(n)\) for \(n\) in the range of \(g\), and to \(\varnothing\)
otherwise, would be a surjection \(\N\to\mathcal P(\N)\), contrary to
\cref{thm:p01-cantor}.  So \(\mathcal P(\N)\) admits no injection into
\(\N\).

Finally, an algorithm reads finite strings over a finite input alphabet
\(\Sigma\).  Replacing each character by a fixed-width binary block, as in
\cref{def:p02-sat-taut}, injects \(\Sigma^{*}\) into \(\{0,1\}^{*}\).  An
algorithm with \(\operatorname{Form}(P)\) as its input domain would
require an injective representation of formulas by strings in
\(\Sigma^{*}\), hence an injection
\(\operatorname{Form}(P)\to\{0,1\}^{*}\), and then \(P\) would be
well-orderable and inject into \(\N\).
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p02-w02-p02-017-infinite-undecidable}{thm:p02-w02-p02-017-infinite-undecidable}{Satisfiability of decidable infinite premise sets is undecidable}
\begin{proof}
Use the relation \(T\) of (S2).  For
\(y\in\N\) put
\[
 \theta_y=\neg p_0\land(p_{y+1}\lor\neg p_{y+1}),
 \qquad
 \Gamma_x=\{p_0\}\cup\{\theta_y:T(x,y)\}.
\]

\emph{Uniform decidability.}  The function \(t(y)=\ulcorner\theta_y\urcorner\)
is computable: a halting machine writes \(\operatorname{bin}(y+1)\),
surrounds it with the fixed characters of the formula string of
\(\theta_y\), applies the encoding of \cref{def:p02-sat-taut}, and
prefixes the digit \(1\); the result is the numeral of \(t(y)\).  By
(S1), \(t(y)>y+1>y\).  Define by primitive
recursion
\[
 B(x,n,0)=0,\qquad
 B(x,n,y+1)=\max\bigl(B(x,n,y),\
   \operatorname{eq}(n,t(y))\cdot\operatorname{char}_T(x,y)\bigr).
\]
Then \(B(x,n,m)=1\) iff some \(y<m\) has \(n=t(y)\) and \(T(x,y)\).  Put
\[
 M(x,n)=\max\bigl(\operatorname{eq}(n,\ulcorner p_0\urcorner),\
   B(x,n,n+1)\bigr),
\]
a computable function by the closure facts.  Since
\(\alpha\mapsto\ulcorner\alpha\urcorner\) is injective, \(n\) is the code
of a member of \(\Gamma_x\) iff \(n=\ulcorner p_0\urcorner\) or
\(n=t(y)\) for some \(y\) with \(T(x,y)\); in the latter case
\(y<t(y)=n<n+1\), so the bounded search finds \(y\).  Hence \(M\) is the
characteristic function of
\(\{(x,\ulcorner\gamma\urcorner):\gamma\in\Gamma_x\}\).  For fixed \(x\),
\(n\mapsto M(x,n)\) is computable, so each \(\Gamma_x\) is decidable.

\emph{Satisfiability.}  If \(x\notin K\), no \(y\) satisfies \(T(x,y)\)
by (S2), so \(\Gamma_x=\{p_0\}\), which
the valuation with every value \(1\) satisfies.  If \(x\in K\), fix a
\(y\) with \(T(x,y)\).  Then \(p_0,\theta_y\in\Gamma_x\), and no valuation
makes both \(p_0\) and \(\neg p_0\) true, so \(\Gamma_x\) is
unsatisfiable.

\emph{Consequences.}  Thus \(\{x:\Gamma_x\text{ is satisfiable}\}=
\N\setminus K\).  By the corollary following
\cref{thm:halting-undecidable} in \cref{sec:universal-reductions-03}, this
set is not computably enumerable.  If it were decidable, the characteristic function
of \(K\), which is \(x\mapsto1\mathbin{\dot{-}}\operatorname{char}_{\N\setminus
K}(x)\), would be computable, contrary to
\cref{thm:halting-undecidable}.  A finite subset of \(\Gamma_x\) is a
finite subset of \(\operatorname{Form}(P_{\N})\), so it has a finite encoded input over the
identity coding of its variables, on which \cref{thm:p02-decidability}
decides satisfiability.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p02-w02-p02-017-no-computable-valuation}{thm:p02-w02-p02-017-no-computable-valuation}{A decidable satisfiable premise set with no computable model}
\begin{proof}
Use \(F\), \(e^{*}\) and \(T\) of (S2).

\emph{Unique witnesses.}  Define by primitive recursion
\[
 N(x,0)=1,\qquad
 N(x,y+1)=N(x,y)\cdot\bigl(1\mathbin{\dot{-}}\operatorname{char}_T(x,y)\bigr),
\]
so \(N(x,y)=1\) iff no \(z<y\) satisfies \(T(x,z)\).  Let \(W(x,y)\) hold
iff \(T(x,y)\) and \(N(x,y)=1\); its characteristic function
\(\operatorname{char}_T\cdot N\) is computable.  If \(W(x,y)\) and
\(W(x,y')\) with \(y<y'\), then \(N(x,y')=1\) contradicts \(T(x,y)\); so
each \(x\) has at most one \(y\) with \(W(x,y)\), namely the least \(y\)
with \(T(x,y)\) when there is one.  By the normal form,
\begin{equation}
 W(x,y)\iff F(x)\text{ is defined and }y=\mu z\,T(x,z),
 \qquad\text{and then } F(x)=\mathsf U(y).
 \tag{S3}
\end{equation}

\emph{The premise set.}  Put \(\tau_y=p_{2y+1}\lor\neg p_{2y+1}\) and
\[
 \delta_{x,y}=
 \begin{cases}
  \neg p_{2x}\land\tau_y, & \mathsf U(y)=0,\\
  p_{2x}\land\tau_y, & \mathsf U(y)\ne0,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad
 \Delta=\{\delta_{x,y}:W(x,y)\}.
\]

\emph{Decidability.}  The functions
\(d_0(x,y)=\ulcorner\neg p_{2x}\land\tau_y\urcorner\) and
\(d_1(x,y)=\ulcorner p_{2x}\land\tau_y\urcorner\) are computable in the
same way as \(t\) in the preceding proof, and \(\mathsf U\) is primitive
recursive.  Hence
\[
 d(x,y)=\operatorname{eq}(\mathsf U(y),0)\cdot d_0(x,y)
 +\bigl(1\mathbin{\dot{-}}\operatorname{eq}(\mathsf U(y),0)\bigr)\cdot d_1(x,y)
 =\ulcorner\delta_{x,y}\urcorner
\]
is computable.  Since \(p_{2x}\) and \(p_{2y+1}\) occur in
\(\delta_{x,y}\), (S1) gives
\(d(x,y)>2x\ge x\) and \(d(x,y)>2y+1>y\).  Define by primitive recursion
\[
\begin{gathered}
 C(n,x,0)=0,\qquad
 C(n,x,y+1)=\max\bigl(C(n,x,y),\
   \operatorname{char}_W(x,y)\cdot\operatorname{eq}(n,d(x,y))\bigr),\\
 D(n,0)=0,\qquad
 D(n,x+1)=\max\bigl(D(n,x),\ C(n,x,n+1)\bigr).
\end{gathered}
\]
Then \(D(n,n+1)=1\) iff some \(x,y\le n\) satisfy \(W(x,y)\) and
\(n=d(x,y)\).  By injectivity of code numbers, \(n\) codes a member of
\(\Delta\) iff \(n=d(x,y)\) for some \((x,y)\) with \(W(x,y)\), and then
\(x,y<n\).  So \(n\mapsto D(n,n+1)\) is the characteristic function of
\(\{\ulcorner\delta\urcorner:\delta\in\Delta\}\), and \(\Delta\) is
decidable.

\emph{Satisfiability without choice.}  Define the valuation \(v\) on
\(P_{\N}\) by \(v(p_{2x})=1\) iff \(x\in K\) and \(F(x)\ne0\), and
\(v(p_{2y+1})=0\).  It is given by an explicit definition, so no choice
principle is used.  Every \(\tau_y\) is true under every valuation.  Let
\(\delta_{x,y}\in\Delta\), so \(W(x,y)\); by
(S3), \(x\in K\) and
\(F(x)=\mathsf U(y)\).  If \(\mathsf U(y)=0\), then \(F(x)=0\), so
\(v(p_{2x})=0\) and \(\neg p_{2x}\land\tau_y\) is true.  If
\(\mathsf U(y)\ne0\), then \(F(x)\ne0\), so \(v(p_{2x})=1\) and
\(p_{2x}\land\tau_y\) is true.  Hence \(v\) satisfies \(\Delta\).

\emph{No computable model.}  Suppose a valuation \(w\) satisfies
\(\Delta\) and \(n\mapsto w(p_n)\) is computable.  Then
\(h(x)=1\mathbin{\dot{-}} w(p_{2x})\) is computable and total.  By
\cref{thm:enumeration}(b) there is an index \(b\) with
\(\varphi_b\simeq h\).  Then \(\varphi_b(b)=h(b)\) is defined, so
\(F(b)=h(b)\), \(b\in K\), and by (S3)
there is a \(y\) with \(W(b,y)\) and \(\mathsf U(y)=h(b)\).  So
\(\delta_{b,y}\in\Delta\).  If \(h(b)=0\), then \(\delta_{b,y}=\neg
p_{2b}\land\tau_y\), so \(w(p_{2b})=0\) and \(h(b)=1\).  If \(h(b)=1\),
then \(\mathsf U(y)\ne0\), \(\delta_{b,y}=p_{2b}\land\tau_y\), so
\(w(p_{2b})=1\) and \(h(b)=0\).  Both cases are contradictory, so no
computable valuation satisfies \(\Delta\).
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p02-w02-p02-017-bpi-boundary}{thm:p02-w02-p02-017-bpi-boundary}{Finite checks supply the hypothesis, not the valuation}
\begin{proof}
\emph{Clause 1.}  Apply
\cref{thm:p02-w02-p02-017-finite-reduction}(2) to each finite
\(\Gamma_0\subseteq\Gamma\) with \(\varphi=\bottom\), so that
\(A=\operatorname{Var}(\Gamma_0)\).  The check succeeds on \(\Gamma_0\)
exactly when \(\Gamma_0\) is satisfiable.

\emph{Clause 2.}  Let \(c\) be an atom coding of \(P\).  The map
\(\alpha\mapsto\alpha^{c}\) is injective on \(\operatorname{Form}(P)\),
by induction on formulas: atoms go to distinct variables because \(c\) is
injective, and the outermost constructor and immediate subformulas of
\(\alpha\) are recovered from those of \(\alpha^{c}\).  Let \(\Gamma\) be
finitely satisfiable and let \(\Sigma\subseteq\Gamma^{c}\) be finite.
The set \(\Gamma_0=\{\gamma\in\Gamma:\gamma^{c}\in\Sigma\}\) is finite,
since translation maps it injectively into \(\Sigma\), and
\(\Gamma_0^{c}=\Sigma\).  \(\Gamma_0\) is satisfiable, so \(\Sigma\) is
satisfiable by \cref{thm:p02-w02-p02-017-finite-reduction}(3) with
\(Q=P\).  Thus \(\Gamma^{c}\subseteq\operatorname{Form}(P_{\N})\) is finitely satisfiable,
and \cref{thm:prop-compactness}(2) gives a valuation \(u\) satisfying
\(\Gamma^{c}\).  Its partner \(v\) on \(P\) from the same clause~3
satisfies \(\Gamma\).  \Cref{thm:prop-compactness} is proved for the
fixed alphabet \(P_{\N}\) by an explicit enumeration and uses no choice
principle, as recorded in \cref{thm:p01-bpi-propositional-compactness}
and at the opening of \cref{sec:p02-free-boolean-completeness}; the
translation steps are explicit definitions.

\emph{Clause 3, from \(\mathsf{BPI}\).}  Over
\(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{BPI}\), \cref{thm:p02-fbc-completeness} states for
every set \(P\) that every finitely satisfiable set of formulas of
\(\operatorname{Form}(P)\) is satisfiable.

\emph{Clause 3, to \(\mathsf{BPI}\).}  Assume the scheme.  Let \(V\) be a
set and use the language of \cref{def:p01-bpi-propositional-compactness},
with variables \(p_v\) (\(v\in V\)), constants \(\bot,\top\) and
connectives \(\neg,\land,\lor\).  Take \(P=\{p_v:v\in V\}\) as a set of
atoms and translate each formula \(\sigma\) of that language to
\(\sigma^{\bullet}\in\operatorname{Form}(P)\) by
\(p_v^{\bullet}=p_v\), \(\bot^{\bullet}=\bottom\),
\(\top^{\bullet}=\neg\bottom\), and by commuting with
\(\neg,\land,\lor\).  For \(\nu:V\to\mathbf2\) let
\(v_\nu(p_v)=\nu(v)\).  Induction on \(\sigma\) shows that the value of
\(\sigma\) under \(\nu\) equals \(\widehat{v_\nu}(\sigma^{\bullet})\); the
case \(\top\) uses \(\widehat{v_\nu}(\neg\bottom)=1\).  Every valuation
on \(P\) is \(v_\nu\) for exactly one \(\nu\).  Let \(\Sigma\) be finitely
satisfiable in the sense of \cref{def:p01-bpi-propositional-compactness},
and let \(\Phi\subseteq\Sigma^{\bullet}\) be finite.  Each member of
\(\Phi\) has a nonempty set of preimages in \(\Sigma\); a finite family of
nonempty sets has a choice function in \(\mathsf{ZF}\), by induction on
the number of members.  The chosen preimages form a finite
\(\Sigma_0\subseteq\Sigma\), satisfied by some \(\nu\), and then
\(v_\nu\) satisfies \(\Phi\).  So \(\Sigma^{\bullet}\) is finitely
satisfiable, the scheme gives a valuation \(v_\nu\) satisfying it, and
\(\nu\) satisfies \(\Sigma\).  This is the compactness principle of
\cref{def:p01-bpi-propositional-compactness} for every set \(V\), and
\cref{thm:p01-bpi-propositional-compactness} yields \(\mathsf{BPI}\).

\emph{Consequence.}  Suppose \(\mathsf{ZF}\) proved that, for every set
\(P\) and every \(\Gamma\subseteq\operatorname{Form}(P)\), success of all
the finite checks on finite subsets of \(\Gamma\) implies that
\(\Gamma\) is satisfiable.  By clause~1 \(\mathsf{ZF}\) would prove the
scheme of clause~3, and hence \(\mathsf{BPI}\).  In the proof of
\cref{thm:p02-fbc-separation} the countervaluation is
\(v_U=\chi_U\eta_P\), where \(U\) is an ultrafilter extending a
prescribed proper filter; its existence is the single use of
\(\mathsf{BPI}\), through \cref{thm:p01-bpi-equivalence}, and no step of
that proof applies a decision procedure.  When \(P\) has no atom coding,
\cref{thm:p02-w02-p02-017-no-coding} shows that no algorithm even reads
the formulas whose classes form \(L_P\).
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p02-w02-p02-017-pairs}{thm:p02-w02-p02-017-pairs}{Valuations of the pair-selection premises are choice functions}
\begin{proof}
Each \(a\in P\) lies in exactly one member of \(\mathcal A\), by
disjointness; write \(A_a\) for it.  Since every member of
\(\mathcal A\) has two elements, the formulas of \(\Gamma_{\mathcal A}\)
are exactly \((a\lor b)\land\neg(a\land b)\) with \(\{a,b\}\in\mathcal
A\) and \(a\ne b\).  Such a formula is true under \(v\) iff
\(v(a)+v(b)=1\), that is, iff exactly one of \(a,b\) has value \(1\).
This proves the characterization of satisfying valuations.

\emph{Finite subsets.}  Let \(\Gamma_0\subseteq\Gamma_{\mathcal A}\) be
finite.  The map \(a\mapsto A_a\) sends the finite set
\(\operatorname{Var}(\Gamma_0)\) onto
\(\mathcal A_0=\{A\in\mathcal A:A\cap\operatorname{Var}(\Gamma_0)\neq
\varnothing\}\), so \(\mathcal A_0\) is finite.  A finite family of
nonempty sets has a choice function in \(\mathsf{ZF}\): the empty family
has the empty function, and a choice function on \(n\) members extends
to \(n+1\) members by one further choice.  Let \(g\) be a choice
function on \(\mathcal A_0\), and put \(v(a)=1\) iff \(A_a\in\mathcal A_0\)
and \(a=g(A_a)\).  Every formula of \(\Gamma_0\) has the form displayed
above with \(\{a,b\}\in\mathcal A_0\), and exactly one of \(a,b\), namely
\(g(\{a,b\})\), has value \(1\).  So \(v\) satisfies \(\Gamma_0\).

\emph{The bijection.}  For a satisfying valuation \(v\), let \(g_v(A)\)
be the unique \(a\in A\) with \(v(a)=1\); this defines a choice function
on \(\mathcal A\) by separation, without any choice.  For a choice
function \(g\) on \(\mathcal A\), put \(v_g(a)=1\) iff \(a=g(A_a)\); it
gives value \(1\) to exactly one element of each member, so it satisfies
\(\Gamma_{\mathcal A}\).  Then \(g_{v_g}=g\), and \(v_{g_v}=v\) because
\(v(a)=1\) iff \(a\) is the element of \(A_a\) with value \(1\).

\emph{Under \(\mathsf{BPI}\).}  The set \(\Gamma_{\mathcal A}\) is
finitely satisfiable, so over \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{BPI}\) it is
satisfiable by \cref{thm:p02-fbc-completeness}, and the bijection turns a
satisfying valuation into a choice function on \(\mathcal A\).  The case
\(\mathcal A=\varnothing\) is included: then \(P\) and
\(\Gamma_{\mathcal A}\) are empty, and the empty valuation corresponds to
the empty choice function.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}
